'''''Hibiscus tiliaceus''''', commonly known as the '''sea hibiscus''' or '''coast cottonwood''', is an evergreen species of [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[tree]] in the [[Malva|mallow]] family, [[Malvaceae]], with a [[pantropical]] distribution along coastlines. It has also been introduced to [[Florida]] and [[New Zealand]]. It has been debated whether this species is native or introduced to [[Hawaii]].<ref name="iucn" />

== Names ==
Common names include '''sea hibiscus''', '''beach hibiscus''', '''coastal''' (or '''coast''') '''hibiscus''', '''coastal''' (or '''coast''') '''cottonwood''', '''green cottonwood''', '''native hibiscus''', '''native rosella''', '''cottonwood hibiscus''', '''kurrajong''', '''sea rosemallow''' and '''dhigga''' ([[Maldivian language|Maldivian]]).

The plant was [[Domesticated plants and animals of Austronesia#Talipariti tiliaceum (sea hibiscus)|introduced]] {{where|date=July 2024}} by [[Austronesian peoples]] that voyaged across Southeast Asia and Oceania as a source of wood and fibre.<ref name="Prebble2012">{{cite book|first1=Matiu |last1=Prebble|first2=Atholl |last2=Anderson|editor1-first=Atholl |editor1-link=Atholl Anderson |editor1-last=Anderson |editor2-first=Douglas J. |editor2-last=Kennett|title =Taking the High Ground: The archaeology of Rapa, a fortified island in remote East Polynesia|chapter =The archaeobotany of Rapan rockshelter deposits|publisher =ANU E Press|series =terra australis|volume=37|year =2012|pages=77–95|isbn =978-1-922144-25-6|chapter-url =http://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p204851/pdf/ch043.pdf}}</ref><ref name="Dotte-Sarout2017">{{cite journal |last1=Dotte-Sarout |first1=Emilie |last2=Kahn |first2=Jennifer G. |title=Ancient woodlands of Polynesia: A pilot anthracological study on Maupiti Island, French Polynesia |journal=Quaternary International |date=November 2017 |volume=457 |pages=6–28 |doi=10.1016/j.quaint.2016.10.032|bibcode=2017QuInt.457....6D }}</ref> This is reflected in the names of the plant as spoken in many [[Austronesian languages|related languages]] spoken in those regions including  '''''balibago''''' ([[Tagalog language|Tagalog]]), 
'''''malobago''''' ([[Central Bikol|Bikol]]), '''''malabago''''' or '''''malbago''''' ([[Cebuano language|Cebuano]] – Southern), '''''maribago''''' ([[Cebuano language|Cebuano]] – Northern), '''''lambago''''' (Cebuano - Cagayan de Oro), '''''waru''''' ([[Sundanese language|Sundanese]] & [[Javanese language|Javanese]]), '''''varo''''' ([[Malagasy language|Malagasy]]), '''''baru''''' or '''''bebaru''''' ([[Malay language|Malay]]), '''''pagu''''' ([[Chamorro language|Chamorro]]), '''''hau''''' ([[Hawaiian language|Hawaiian]]),  '''''fau''''' ([[Samoan language|Samoan]]), '''''purau''''' ([[Tahitian language|Tahitian]]), and '''vau tree''' ([[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://acd.clld.org/cognatesets/25187#2/-10.1/153.8|title=*baRu: a small shore tree: Hibiscus tiliaceus|last1=Blust|first1=Robert|last2=Trussel|first2=Stephen|website=Austronesian Comparative Dictionary|date=2010|publisher=Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology|access-date=30 September 2022}}</ref> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]], ''"tiliaceus"'', refers to its resemblance of the leaves to those of the related ''[[Tilia]]'' species.<ref name="WHPNA">{{cite web |url=http://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/invweed/WeedsHI/W_Hibiscus_tiliaceus.pdf |first=P. |last=Motooka |author2=L. Castro |author3=D. Nelson |author4=G. Nagai |author5= L. Ching  |title=Hibiscus tiliaceus Hau |work=Weeds of Hawaiʻi's Pastures and Natural Areas; An Identification and Management Guide |publisher=University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa |access-date=2010-02-16}}</ref>

==Description==
''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' reaches a height of {{convert|4|-|10|m|ft|abbr=on}}, with a trunk up to {{convert|15|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name="CFTH"/> The [[flower]]s of ''H. tiliaceus'' are bright yellow with a deep red center upon opening. Over the course of the day, the flowers deepen to orange and finally red before they fall. The branches of the tree often curve over time. The leaves are heart shaped and deep red in the var. ''rubra''.

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Hibiscus pernambucensis.jpg|thumb|''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' subsp. ''pernambucensis'' in [[Brazil]]]]
''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' has a worldwide tropical distribution. In the [[Old World]] and [[Oceania]], it is a common [[coast]]al plant in most of tropical [[Africa]], [[South Asia]] (including the [[Maldives]]), [[Southeast Asia]], parts of [[East Asia]] (as far north as central [[Japan]], where it reaches its northernmost extent), eastern and northern [[Australia]],<ref name="plantnet">{{cite web |title=''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Hibiscus~tiliaceus |access-date=29 January 2019 |work=PlantNET - NSW Flora Online}}</ref> and much of the [[List of islands in the Pacific Ocean|Pacific Islands]], including [[Hawaii]] (where its establishment status is uncertain). It has also been introduced to [[New Zealand]]. A separate subspecies, ''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' subsp. ''pernambucensis'' (formerly considered a separate species, ''H. pernambucensis''), is native to the tropical [[New World]], including [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], the [[Caribbean]], and much of [[South America]].<ref name = pernambucensis/> This variety has also been introduced to [[Florida]].<ref name="iucn" /><ref name="CFTH">{{cite web |last=Little Jr. |first=Elbert L. |author2=Roger G. Skolmen |year=1989 |title=Hau, sea hibiscus |url=http://www2.ctahr.hawaii.edu/forestry/trees/CommonTreesHI/CFT_Hibiscus_tiliaceus.pdf |access-date=2010-02-16 |work=Common Forest Trees of Hawaii (Native and Introduced) |publisher=United States Forest Service}}</ref>

It is uncertain if the species is native to Hawaii, as it may have been [[canoe plants|introduced by Polynesians]].<ref name="WHPNA" /> It is considered native by [[Plants of the World Online]], but the IUCN considers it of uncertain status.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30143354-2 |access-date=2022-06-27 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref name="iucn" /> ''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' can be found at elevations from sea level to {{convert|800|m|ft|abbr=on}} in areas that receive {{convert|900|–|2500|mm|in|abbr=on}} of annual rainfall. It is commonly found growing on [[beach]]es, [[riparian zone|by rivers]], and in [[mangrove forests]]. Sea hibiscus is well adapted to grow in coastal environment as it [[halophyte|tolerates salt]] and waterlogging and can grow in [[quartz]] sand, [[coral sand]], [[marl]], [[limestone]],<ref name="TradTree">{{cite web |last=Elevitch |first=Craig R. |author2=Lex A.J. Thomson |date=April 2006 |title=''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' (beach hibiscus) |url=http://www.agroforestry.net/tti/H.tiliaceus-beach-hibiscus.pdf |publisher=The Traditional Tree Initiative}}</ref> and crushed [[basalt]].<ref name="RNGR">{{cite web |last=Allen |first=James A. |date=2003-01-01 |title=''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' L. |url=http://www.rngr.net/publications/ttsm/species/PDF.2004-03-03.4433/at_download/file |access-date=2009-03-01 |work=Tropical Tree Seed Manual |publisher=Reforestation, Nurseries & Genetics Resources |format=PDF}}</ref> It grows best in slightly [[acid]]ic to [[alkali]]ne soils ([[soil pH]] of 5–8.5).<ref name="TradTree" />
[[Cotton Tree, Queensland]], Australia and [[Balibago]], Angeles, Philippines are named for the plant.

==Uses==
[[File:Starr 020803-0107 Hibiscus tiliaceus.jpg|thumb|left|Sea hibiscus from [[Hawaii]]]]
The wood of ''H. tiliaceus'' has a [[specific gravity]] of 0.6. It has been used in a variety of applications, such as seacraft construction, [[firewood]], and [[wood carving]]s. It is easy to plane and turns well, so it is regarded by many as a high quality furniture wood. Plant fibers taken from the stems have traditionally been used in [[rope]] making,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Standley |first1=Paul C. |author-link1=Paul Carpenter Standley |last2=Blake |first2=S. F. |author-link2=Sidney Fay Blake |title=Trees and Shrubs of Mexico (Oxalidaceae-Turneraceae)|journal=Contributions from the United States National Herbarium |publisher=Department of Botany, [[Smithsonian Institution]]|volume=23 |issue=3 |location=Washington, D.C.|page=780|date=1923|jstor=23492504 }}</ref> while its bark has been used like cork, in sealing cracks in boats. The bark and roots may be boiled to make a cooling tea to cool [[fever]]s, and its young leafy [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s may be eaten as vegetables. [[Native Hawaiians]] used the wood to make ''[[Aka (sailing)|{{okina}}iako]]'' (spars) for ''wa{{okina}}a'' ([[outrigger canoe]]s), ''mouo'' ([[fishing net]] floats), and ''{{okina}}au ko{{okina}}i'' ([[adze]] handles). ''Kaula {{okina}}ilihau'' (cordage) was made from the [[bast fibre|bast fiber]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www2.bishopmuseum.org/ethnobotanydb/resultsdetailed.asp?search=hau |title=hau, hau kaʻekaʻe |publisher=Bernice P. Bishop Museum |work=Hawaii Ethnobotany Online Database |access-date=2009-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070702123224/http://www2.bishopmuseum.org/ethnobotanydb/resultsdetailed.asp?search=hau |archive-date=2007-07-02 }}</ref>  ''Hau'' would be used to make ''[[Ama (sailing)|{{okina}}ama]]'' (canoe floats) if the preferred ''[[wiliwili]]'' (''Erythrina sandwicensis'') was unavailable.<ref name="Auwahi">{{cite web |url=http://www.hear.org/naturalareas/auwahi/ethnobotany_of_auwahi.pdf |title=Auwahi: Ethnobotany of a Hawaiian Dryland Forest |first=A. C. |last=Medeiros |author2=C.F. Davenport |author3=C.G. Chimera  |publisher=Cooperative National Park Resources Studies Unit, [[University of Hawaii at Manoa|University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa]] |year=1998}}</ref>

''Hibiscus tiliaceus'' is widely used in Asian countries, especially Taiwan, as a subject for the art of [[bonsai]]. The finest specimens are taken from [[Kenting National Park]]. Lending itself to free [[grafting]], the leaf size is reduced fairly quickly.  Its leaves are also used in cooking, as trays for steamed rice cakes ([[Caozaiguo|粿]]).

In [[Indonesia]] ''H. tiliaceus'' is also used for fermenting [[tempeh]]. The undersides of the leaves are covered in downy hairs known technically as trichomes to which the mold ''[[Rhizopus oligosporus]]'' can be found adhering in the wild. [[Soybeans]] are pressed into the leaf, and stored. Fermentation occurs resulting in tempeh.<ref name="The Book of Tempeh">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hdKzFlaqWT8C |format=PDF |title=The Book of Tempeh |first=William |last=Shirtleff |author2=Akiko Aoyagi  |publisher=Soyinfo Center, [[Harper and Row]] |year=1979|isbn=978-0-06-014009-0 }}</ref>

Indigenous Australians traditionally used the inner bark of the tree to craft fishing nets and ropes, particularly for use with dugong and turtle harpoons. The wood was also employed in the making of shields. Medicinally, the inner bark and sapwood were soaked in water and heated with hot stones, producing a liquid that was applied to wash wounds. Strips of bark were additionally used as natural bandages, wrapped around injuries to cover and close them.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Petrie |first=Constance |title=Tom Petrie's Reminiscences of Early Queensland |date= |publisher=Angus and Robertson |year=1975}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Welsby |first=Thomas |title=Recollections of the Natives of Moreton Bay |publisher=University Society (Brisbane) |year=1916}}</ref>

===Chemistry===
[[Chrysanthemin]] (Cyanidin-3-glucoside) is the major [[anthocyanin]] found in flowers of ''H. tiliaceus''.<ref>Lowry, J.B. (1976). "Floral anthocyanins of some Malesian ''Hibiscus'' species". ''Phytochemistry'' '''15''': 1395–1396.</ref> Leaves of ''H. tiliaceus'' displayed strong free radical scavenging activity and the highest tyrosinase inhibition activity among 39 tropical plant species in [[Okinawa Prefecture]].<ref>(Masuda ''et al''., 1999; 2005)</ref> With greater UV radiation in coastal areas, it is possible that leaves and flowers of natural coastal populations of ''H. tiliaceus'' have stronger antioxidant properties than planted inland populations.<ref>(Wong ''et al''., 2009; Wong & Chan, 2010).</ref>
